title: The personal infinitive
objectives: I can explain what the personal infinitive is and why Portuguese marks on the infinitive who does the action.
I can form falares, falarmos and falarem for regular and irregular verbs, and I know why saírem carries an accent.
I can decide whether an infinitive has its own doer and so needs its ending, or shares the doer of the main verb and stays plain.
I can use the personal infinitive after prepositions such as antes de, depois de, sem, para, por and ao.
I can read formal notices and rules that use it, and I know the everyday alternatives such as pra gente sair and the subjunctive.

vocabulary.note: The ending -dade is the usual way to turn an adjective into an abstract noun (responsável, responsible). The stress is res-pon-sa-bi-li-DA-de, on the second to last syllable, because the ending e predicts that, so no accent is written. The last de is said like English 'jee' because d before a weak final e sounds like j in 'jeans'.

example.pt: Cada membro da equipe tem a sua responsabilidade.
example.en: Each member of the team has their own responsibility.
example.literal: Each member of-the team has the its responsibility.

vocabulary.note: A piece of work assigned to someone. Dividir as tarefas, to share out the tasks, is the fixed phrase for splitting up work in a group.

example.pt: A primeira tarefa é preparar a apresentação.
example.en: The first task is to prepare the presentation.

vocabulary.note: Equipe is e-QUI-pe: qu before i is [k] with a silent u, and the final e is said like i. Equipa is the European form.

example.pt: A equipe trabalhou até tarde para terminar o projeto.
example.en: The team worked late to finish the project.
example.literal: The team worked until late for to-finish the project.

vocabulary.note: A person who shares your workplace, class or team. The ending -a does not make it feminine: o colega is a man and a colega is a woman, the same word with a different article. Stress is on the second to last syllable (co-LE-ga).

example.pt: Meu colega de trabalho me ajudou com o relatório.
example.en: My coworker helped me with the report.
example.literal: My colleague of work me helped with the report.

vocabulary.note: The feminine is a funcionária. Fun-ci-o-NÁ-rio: the ending io counts as two syllables for the stress rule, so the stress is on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, and the acute accent is written. The ç is not needed: c before i is already [s].

example.pt: Os funcionários novos começam na segunda-feira.
example.en: The new employees start on Monday.
example.literal: The employees new begin on-the second-fair.

vocabulary.note: The feminine is a estagiária. Es-ta-gi-Á-rio is accented for the same reason as funcionário (ending io, stress third to last). The gi is [ʒi], the j of 'measure'. It comes from o estágio, internship, es-TÁ-gi-o.

example.pt: A estagiária aprendeu muito nos primeiros meses.
example.en: The intern learned a lot in the first months.
example.literal: The intern learned much in-the first months.

vocabulary.note: For a report, an exam, a package or keys: entregar o relatório ao chefe, to hand the report to the boss. The r at the end is weak in speech, but in the personal infinitive it moves inside the word and is pronounced: entregarmos, entregarem.

example.pt: Preciso entregar o relatório até sexta.
example.en: I need to hand in the report by Friday.
example.literal: I-need to-hand-in the report until Friday.

vocabulary.note: Used for deadlines, rules, promises and duties: cumprir o prazo, cumprir as regras. The m of cum closes the syllable, so it only nasalizes the u. Stress is on the last syllable (cum-PRIR), as the ending r predicts.

example.pt: Para cumprir o prazo, vamos trabalhar no sábado.
example.en: To meet the deadline, we are going to work on Saturday.
example.literal: For to-fulfill the deadline, we-go to-work on-the Saturday.

vocabulary.note: Both d's come before i, so both are said [dʒ]: dʒi-vi-DʒIR. It can mean to split into parts or to share a cost or a task.

example.pt: Vamos dividir as tarefas entre os quatro.
example.en: Let's divide the tasks among the four of us.
example.literal: We-go to-divide the tasks between the four.

vocabulary.note: To pass an official piece of information to someone, with a or ao for the person told. The related noun is o comunicado, a notice. In chefia the ch is [ʃ]; it means the management, the people in charge, and comes from o chefe, the boss.

example.pt: Preciso comunicar o atraso à chefia.
example.en: I need to inform management about the delay.
example.literal: I-need to-inform the delay to-the management.

vocabulary.note: Takes a direct object or an infinitive: evitar o trânsito, evitar chegar tarde.

example.pt: Para evitarmos atrasos, vamos sair mais cedo.
example.en: To avoid delays, we are going to leave earlier.
example.literal: For to-avoid-we delays, we-go to-leave more early.

vocabulary.en: to be absent, to be missing
vocabulary.note: Literally to lack, so it covers two situations: a person is absent (faltar à aula, to miss class) or a thing is missing (falta um aluno, one student is missing). Sem falta, literally without lack, means without fail. The l closes the syllable, so it is said [w]: faw-TAR.

example.pt: Ele faltou à aula porque estava doente.
example.en: He missed class because he was sick.
example.literal: He lacked to-the class because he-was sick.

vocabulary.note: Things that run late use atrasar directly (o trem atrasou). For a person, use chegar atrasado, to arrive late, or estar atrasado, to be late. The adjective atrasado agrees with the person (Júlia is atrasada). A single s between two vowels is [z]: a-tra-ZAR.

example.pt: O trem atrasou e eu cheguei tarde.
example.en: The train was late and I arrived late.
example.literal: The train delayed and I arrived late.

vocabulary.note: Written ss between two vowels is [s]. A single s there would be read [z], so the doubled s is what keeps the hissing sound: a-si-NAR with [s].

example.pt: Antes de assinar, leia o contrato com calma.
example.en: Before signing, read the contract calmly.
example.literal: Before of to-sign, read the contract with calm.

vocabulary.note: In school it means how many classes you attended. The qu is an exception: before e, qu is normally [k] with a silent u, but in frequência the u is sounded, [kw]. Until 2009 a trema marked it (freqüência). The ê is closed because the e is followed by n, and the accent is written because the ending ia counts as two syllables and pushes the stress to the third to last. Passar de ano means to be promoted to the next year.

example.pt: A frequência mínima para passar de ano é de setenta e cinco por cento.
example.en: The minimum attendance to move up a grade is seventy-five percent.
example.literal: The attendance minimum for to-pass of year is of seventy and five per hundred.

vocabulary.note: Ma-TRÍ-cu-la: the stress is on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so the acute is written. Fazer a matrícula, literally to make the enrollment, is the normal way to say to enroll.

example.pt: A matrícula para o próximo ano começa em janeiro.
example.en: Enrollment for the next year begins in January.

vocabulary.note: The h is silent. Ho-RÁ-rio takes an accent for the same reason as funcionário. Brazilians often use the 24-hour clock for schedules, so dezoito horas is six in the evening. No horário means on time.

example.pt: O horário de trabalho é das nove às dezoito horas.
example.en: The working hours are from nine to six.
example.literal: The schedule of work is of-the nine to-the eighteen hours.

vocabulary.note: The period of time allowed for something. No prazo is on time, within the deadline, and fora do prazo is late. The z between vowels is [z].

example.pt: A equipe entregou o projeto no prazo.
example.en: The team handed in the project on time.
example.literal: The team handed-in the project in-the deadline.

vocabulary.note: Followed by an infinitive to state a purpose, like para but more formal. The im of fim is a nasal vowel [ĩ]. Colloquially, estar a fim de means to feel like doing something. Trânsito, traffic, takes its circumflex for the reason given in the accent note.

example.pt: Saímos cedo a fim de evitar o trânsito.
example.en: We left early in order to avoid traffic.
example.literal: We-left early to end of to-avoid the traffic.

vocabulary.note: Vez means time in the sense of occasion or turn: uma vez is once, duas vezes is twice, sua vez is your turn. So the phrase says in the turn of. It is followed by a noun or an infinitive.

example.pt: Em vez de reclamarem, eles resolveram ajudar.
example.en: Instead of complaining, they decided to help.
example.literal: In turn of to-complain-they, they resolved to-help.

vocabulary.note: Além alone means beyond or farther. It ends in em but is stressed on the last syllable, which is why it carries the acute, like também.

example.pt: Além de terminarmos o relatório, revisamos tudo.
example.en: Besides finishing the report, we reviewed everything.
example.literal: Beyond of to-finish-we the report, we-reviewed everything.

grammar.title: What the personal infinitive is, and why Portuguese has it
grammar.explanation:
Start with two terms. The subject of a verb is the person or thing that does its action: in Eles querem sair, eles is the subject of both querem (they want) and sair (to leave). A verb form is finite when its ending shows who the subject is and when the action happens: falo, falamos, falaram. The infinitive is the name form of a verb, falar, comer, partir, and it is non-finite: in English, to speak is the same whether the speaker is I, you or they, and the plain Portuguese infinitive is just as blind to the doer.

That blindness is a problem when the infinitive has a doer of its own, different from the subject of the main verb. In I asked them to leave, the main verb has the subject I, but the one who leaves is them. English solves this with word order and with the pronoun form: it puts the doer in the object form (them, us, him) and relies on context, or it turns the verb into an -ing form (without them noticing). Notice that them and us are object forms, even though they do the action: English has no better tool.

Portuguese has one, called the personal infinitive (infinitivo pessoal, also called infinitivo flexionado). To inflect a word is to change its ending to show grammatical information; here the information is the person. The infinitive takes the endings -es for tu, -mos for nós and -em for eles and vocês, and it is used with the subject form of the pronoun: para nós sairmos, pedi para eles esperarem. Nós and eles are subject forms, and the ending agrees with them exactly as the ending of a finite verb would. That agreement is what proves the infinitive really has a subject of its own.

Why does Portuguese need this and English does not? Because Portuguese already marks the person on every finite verb and often drops the subject pronoun (the dropped subject from the first grammar lesson). The ending does the pronoun's job. Antes de chegarmos means before we arrive even with no nós, while English before arriving does not say who arrives. The personal infinitive extends the same habit to the one verb form that would otherwise stay silent. Spanish, French, Italian and English have no infinitive that takes person endings and must use a full clause or rephrase.

Two limits are worth knowing from the start. First, the personal infinitive has no tense of its own; it borrows its time from the main verb, so depois de chegarmos can mean after we arrive or after we arrived, depending on the main verb. Second, when the doer is singular (eu, ele, ela, você, a gente), the form is the bare infinitive, so you cannot see the ending: it is still the personal infinitive, just with nothing to add. The practical difficulty is therefore only for plural doers and for nós.

In the word-for-word lines in this unit, an infinitive carrying an ending is shown with the person attached by a hyphen: to-arrive-we is chegarmos and to-arrive-they is chegarem. The ending -em is the eles form and also serves vocês, because vocês takes third person plural forms.

grammar.title: Forming the personal infinitive
grammar.explanation:
The recipe has one step and no irregular stems: take the whole plain infinitive, including its final r, and add the ending. Tu takes -es, nós takes -mos, and eles, elas and vocês take -em. Eu, ele, ela, você and a gente take nothing, so for them the personal infinitive looks exactly like the plain one. Compare the present tense you learned, where the ending replaces -ar, -er or -ir and depends on the verb family (falo, como, parto). Here nothing is replaced and the family does not matter: falar, comer and partir become falarmos, comermos and partirmos by the same step.

Because the infinitive is added whole, irregular verbs are not irregular here. The irregularity of ser, ir, ter, fazer and ver lives in their stems in other tenses, and the infinitive does not contain the stem: ser gives sermos and serem, ir gives irmos and irem, ter gives termos and terem, fazer gives fazermos and fazerem. This is the most useful fact to remember, because it means you never have to learn a separate table.

Do not confuse it with the future subjunctive. For regular verbs the two look identical (quando falarmos, quando falarem), because the future subjunctive is built from the third person plural of the preterite (falaram, without its -am, gives falar) plus the same endings. For irregular verbs they diverge, and the table shows how: the future subjunctive of ser is for, formos, forem, while the personal infinitive is ser, sermos, serem. The test is the meaning and the context: after quando, se, assim que the subjunctive is used; after a preposition such as antes de, para, sem, the personal infinitive is.

Three further points. First, the stress never moves. Falar is stressed on its last syllable, fa-LAR; in falarmos the same a is still stressed, fa-LAR-mos, and in falarem it is fa-LA-rem, because the r now begins the next syllable. The endings -mos and -em fall under the default stress rule, which puts the stress on the second to last syllable, so no accent is ever needed for them. Second, the one place an accent does appear is in verbs like sair, cair and construir, whose infinitive has a stressed i directly after another vowel. The i alone in its syllable needs an accent; in sair and sairmos the r closes the syllable and no accent is needed, but in saírem the r moves to the next syllable, sa-Í-rem, and the accent is required. The spelling note after this one gives the full logic.

Third, the compound form. Ter plus a participle (a form like falado or chegado, taught with the present perfect) is also an infinitive, and it means having done something. The ending goes on ter, and the participle does not change: por não termos avisado, because we did not warn. The participle stays in -o because it is part of a verb, as in tenho avisado. With ser, the passive, the participle agrees with the subject: para serem aprovados, in order to be approved (plural aprovados because the doers are os alunos).

The tu form (falares, fazeres) is correct wherever people use tu with its own verb forms. Many Brazilians use você instead, which takes the bare infinitive, so the -es forms are the rarest of the four.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: accents and stress in the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every accent in this unit comes from one procedure. Divide the word into syllables (a syllable is one beat of a word, built around a vowel sound), find the stressed syllable by ear, read the default stress from the ending of the word, and write an accent only if the stress disagrees with the default. The mark is then chosen by the vowel: the acute (´) for an open vowel, or for an i or u, which have only one quality; the circumflex (ˆ) for a closed vowel. The tilde (~) is a different mark: it does not show stress but tells you the vowel is nasal, said partly through the nose.

The default has two groups. A word ending in a, e or o, with or without a final s, or in am, em or ens, is stressed on the second to last syllable. A word ending in anything else, including i, u, l, r, z, ã and ão, is stressed on the last. This default already explains the personal infinitive. The plain infinitive ends in r, so it is stressed on its last syllable: fa-LAR. Add the endings -es, -mos and -em and you have endings that belong to the first group, so falares, falarmos and falarem are stressed on the second to last syllable, which is the syllable with the same a as before: fa-LA-res, fa-LAR-mos, fa-LA-rem. They obey their default, so none of them needs a mark.

Group 1: the stress is on the last syllable although the ending predicts the second to last. Você and vocês, até, já, será, além, ninguém and porém all break their default, and so do the one-syllable words é, né (which is não é said fast) and três and nós, which are stressed one-syllable words ending in e, es or os. That is also the whole difference between é (is) and the small word e (and), which is weak and takes no mark. In the words ending in em the e is written with an acute by convention (além, ninguém, porém). The u in ninguém is silent, since gu before e is a hard g.

Group 2: the tilde endings. Ã, ão and ões default to the last syllable, and the tilde already marks the nasal vowel, so nothing more is written: não, então, são, serão, portão, certidão, apresentação, aprovação, atenção, colaboração, reuniões, anotações. In serão the ending ão keeps the stress on the last syllable just as in são.

Group 3: the stress is on the third to last syllable. No ending predicts that, so a mark is always written: sábado, ótimo, última, mínima, próximo, histórico, matrícula, informática, dúvidas, trânsito. The mark is the circumflex when the stressed a, e or o is followed by m or n (trânsito, lâmpada), because that vowel is closed and nasal, and the acute elsewhere. The adjectives in -vel work the same way. The ending l defaults to the last syllable, but flexível and responsável are stressed on the syllable before the vel, so they carry the mark, and so do their plurals, which end in -veis (responsáveis).

Group 4: words that end in a glide (a weak i or u sound) plus a vowel, such as ia, io, ua and uo. For the purpose of the stress rule Portuguese counts the i or u as a syllable of its own, so horário is ho-RÁ-ri-o, stressed on the third to last syllable, and needs a mark. The same holds for funcionário, estagiário, necessário, relatório, prédio, Júlia, frequência, antecedência, diárias and férias. The mark follows the vowel: the circumflex is used when a closed vowel is followed by m or n (frequência, antecedência), and the acute elsewhere (horário, relatório, prédio, férias). Words like responsabilidade are different: they end in a plain e, and the stress is on the second to last syllable.

Group 5: a stressed i that must not merge with the vowel before it. In sair the a and i are two syllables (sa-ir), called a hiatus. The i is stressed, and it is written í when it stands alone in its syllable: saímos (sa-Í-mos), saíram (sa-Í-ram), saírem (sa-Í-rem). It is written plain i when a consonant such as r, l, m, n or z closes the same syllable, or a glide follows it: sair (sa-IR), sairmos (sa-IR-mos), saiu (sa-IU). This explains the contrast between sairmos, with r closing the syllable and no mark, and saírem, where the r moves to the next syllable and the í needs one. The same logic applies to cair and construir.

Three marks have other jobs. The grave accent of à and às is the crase, the preposition a fused with the article a or as. The accent in têm (they have) is a plural marker, distinguishing it from tem (he has), which sound the same in Brazilian speech. Crianças has no tilde because the n after the a already nasalizes it.

Worked example, necessário. Divide it: ne-ces-sá-ri-o. The ending io counts as two syllables, and the stress falls on sá, the third to last. No ending predicts that, so a mark is required. The stressed a is followed by r, so it is open, and the mark is the acute: necessário. Compare necessidade, which ends in e and is stressed on the second to last, da, so it has none.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: consonants, vowels and letter groups in the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese spelling is a code in which something you can see decides the sound: the letter that comes next, the position in the word, or a mark. This note reads the rest of the unit's new words with that code. Sounds are given in square brackets, the International Phonetic Alphabet, and compared with English where there is a match. The table lists each pattern once with words from this unit.

The hard and soft letters. The letter c is [k] before a, o and u and [s] before e and i; g is [g] before a, o and u and [ʒ] (the s of 'measure') before e and i. To get the hard sound before e or i, write qu or gu with a silent u: que, porque, equipe, esquecer, quintal, quero; conseguir; and this is why chegar becomes cheguei, so that the g stays hard before the e. To get [s] before a, o or u, write ç, c with a cedilla (the small hook underneath): começa, março, presença, crianças, peço, façam. A ç never comes at the start of a word. The letter j is always [ʒ]: janeiro, hoje, junto, projeto, haja. After q, a u before a or o is pronounced [w]: quando, quatro. A few words keep a sounded u even before e or i, and a trema (two dots) used to mark them until the spelling agreement of 2009 removed it: frequência and tranquilidade. You learn these words one by one.

The endings -ção and -ções turn verbs into nouns naming the act or the result (apresentar, apresentação; aprovar, aprovação), and are said with the nasal diphthong you met in pão, stressed on the last syllable. The plural -ções, as in anotações, is said [sõjs]. The ending -ões without the c, as in reuniões, is the same nasal glide.

Digraphs, pairs of letters that spell one sound. Ch is [ʃ], the sh of shoe: chegar, chefia, chateado, fecha, chamados, chover. Lh is [ʎ], like the lli of million: trabalhou. Nh is [ɲ], like the ny of canyon: vizinhas. Rr is the strong r, a sound in the back of the throat, like a rough English h: erros, corredor, sobrecarregado. A single r at the start of a word is also strong (relatório, regras, registrar), and between vowels it is a single tap, as in hora. H on its own is always silent: hoje, hora, horário, haja, histórico.

S and z. A single s between two vowels is [z]: atrasar, revisa, avisado, usarem. To write [s] between vowels, double it: disse, isso, assinar, interessados, necessário, pessoal. Z is [z] between vowels (prazo, fazer, vezes, fizemos, prezados). An s that closes a syllable before a voiceless consonant such as t or c is [s] in most of Brazil and [ʃ] in Rio de Janeiro and some other regions: estagiário, escola, esquecer.

The letter x has several sounds and no spelling rule chooses among them. Before a consonant it is [s]: sexta, explicar. After ei it is [ʃ]: deixei, deixarem. In próximo and trouxe it is [s]. In flexível it is [ks]. Learn each word with its sound.

T and d, l, r and the final vowels. In most of Brazil t becomes [tʃ] (like ch in cheese) and d becomes [dʒ] (like j in jeans) before the sound [i], and a final unstressed e is said [i]: gente, cliente, tarde, ótimo, dividir, prédio, responsabilidade. An l that closes a syllable is [w]: algum, alguma, faltar, calma. Unstressed final vowels are weak: a is [ɐ], o is [u] and e is [i], so tarefa, prazo and equipe end in a short a, oo and ee sound. A final r is weak and often dropped in speech, but inside the personal infinitive it is fully pronounced: fa-LAR-mos, fa-LA-rem. Its sound depends on region (a tap, or a stronger sound at the end of a syllable).

Nasal vowels. A vowel followed by m or n that closes its syllable is nasal, and the m or n is not pronounced as a consonant: cumprir, entregar, mensagem, combinado, tranquilidade, departamento. An n that opens a syllable is an ordinary consonant: ano, janeiro, nenhuma. The verb endings are nasal diphthongs too: -am, as in começam and assinam, is said like ão but weakly, and -em, as in falarem, chegarem and devem, is [ẽj̃], like 'ayn' through the nose.

The endings of the personal infinitive sound as they are spelled: -mos is [mus], -es is [is] and -em is [ẽj̃]. No letter in them changes a consonant, so nothing in the infinitive before the ending needs respelling, unlike the subjunctive, where chegar needs chegue.

grammar.title: Whose action is it? When the infinitive needs its own ending
grammar.explanation:
One question decides everything: who performs the action of the infinitive? If it is the same person as the subject of the main verb, and the two verbs work together as one unit, the infinitive stays plain. If the infinitive has a different doer, or a doer who needs to be named, it takes the personal ending. Compare Eles querem sair, where eles both want and leave, with Pedi para eles saírem, where I ask and they leave.

The first kind involves auxiliary and modal verbs. An auxiliary verb is one that helps another verb say when or how something happens; a modal verb says ability, duty or wish. Here they are ir (vão sair), poder, dever, precisar, querer, ter que, começar a and acabar de. With them the subject is shared and the verb group counts as a single unit of meaning, so in ordinary use the second verb stays plain: Eles devem chegar cedo, Eles podem entrar, Eles vão sair. Writing devem chegarem is one of the most common errors learners make after studying this form.

The second kind is the different doer, and it often hides. In Pedi aos alunos para entregarem o trabalho, the students are the indirect object of pedi (the ones I asked), but they are also the ones who hand in, so they are the subject of entregarem and the ending is -em. The test is always who does it, not what grammatical role the word has in the main clause. The same holds after dizer, proibir and permitir: Permiti aos alunos saírem mais cedo.

Impersonal expressions such as é importante, é necessário, é melhor, é possível, é pena and é bom make a judgment without naming a doer. Followed by a bare infinitive they are general: É importante chegar cedo means arriving early is important, for anyone. To say for whom, add the doer and the ending: É importante chegarmos cedo, É importante os pais conhecerem as regras. This is how the personal infinitive adds precision to a general statement.

With a singular doer the form looks plain (É melhor ele esperar, para ninguém esquecer), so the real work is only with nós and plural doers. Verbs of perception (ver, ouvir, sentir) and of causation (deixar, mandar, fazer) are a special case. With a noun as the doer, both forms occur: Vi os meninos entrar is traditional, and Vi os meninos entrarem is also common and fully accepted. With an object pronoun (me, o, a, os, as, nos) the plain form is the rule, because the pronoun belongs to the main verb: Eu as vi brincar.

Finally, after a preposition, when the subject is the same as the main verb's, the ending is optional. You can say Depois de terminar, saímos or Depois de terminarmos, saímos. The inflected form is more explicit and is preferred in formal writing, especially when the infinitive clause comes first and no subject is named, because the ending then tells the reader who is acting.

grammar.title: After prepositions: time, reason, purpose and more
grammar.explanation:
A clause is a group of words built around a verb, and a subordinate clause is one that depends on another, like because we were late. English and Portuguese both use a preposition plus an infinitive form to pack a whole subordinate clause into a few words. Portuguese does it with very little loss, because the personal infinitive keeps the doer: Antes de eles chegarem does the work of the full clause antes que eles cheguem (before they arrive), using the preposition de rather than a conjunction with the subjunctive.

Prepositions in this pattern fall into groups by what they express. Time: antes de, depois de, ao, até. Reason: por. Purpose: para, a fim de. Manner and addition: sem, em vez de, além de, apesar de. The pattern is always the preposition, then the doer if it needs naming, then the infinitive with its ending: para terminarmos no prazo, sem vocês ajudarem, por eles não cumprirem o prazo.

Ao deserves an explanation because it is unique. It is the preposition a joined to the article o, and here the infinitive works as a noun: ao chegarem is at the arriving, that is, at the moment they arrive. It means upon doing something or when it happens: Ao chegarem, os alunos assinam a lista.

There is one rule that trips up even native writers. When the doer is a subject pronoun (ele, ela, eles, elas), the preposition de is kept apart from it: antes de ele chegar, depois de eles saírem. Dele and deles are the contractions of de plus ele or eles, and they also mean his and theirs, which is why careful writers avoid them here. In casual speech antes dele chegar is common; in formal writing many style guides treat it as an error. The same rule applies to articles: with a noun as the doer, write depois de os alunos chegarem, not depois dos alunos chegarem, because os belongs to the subject and not to the preposition.

Negation is placed before the infinitive, as before any verb, not before the preposition: por não termos avisado, para não chegarmos atrasados. An object pronoun such as nos or me stays before the inflected infinitive in speech: sem eles nos ajudarem.

If the doer is the same as the subject of the main verb, the ending is optional, as the previous note explained. When the two doers differ, the ending and, in most cases, the pronoun are needed. Notice how much shorter the result is than the clause it replaces.

grammar.title: Small words and fixed phrases in the dialogues: literal meaning and use
grammar.explanation:
Several phrases in the dialogues say something different from what their words add up to. The table gives two things separately: what each phrase says word for word and what it means in natural English. The paragraphs explain how each is used. Thinking in the literal version first helps you remember the structure.

Seu Roberto. Seu is a shortened senhor (sir), used before a first name as a polite, friendly title for an older man; dona plays the same role for women (dona Maria). It is not the possessive seu (your), which is spelled the same. Pessoal means personnel in the sense of the people in a group, and o pessoal is the everyday way to say everyone, the gang, the team. A gente is literally the people and means we, with a third person singular verb (a gente precisa). Combinado is the participle of combinar (to combine), and it is the standard way to confirm an agreement: literally combined, meaning agreed, deal.

Verbs of doing and staying. Fazer in fazer a matrícula and fazer a prova (to take an exam) is make or do in the sense of carrying out a procedure. Ficar com means to stay with, which in a project becomes to take charge of: Eu e a Ana ficamos com o relatório. Ficar plus an adjective of feeling or state means to become it: ficar nervoso, ficar chateado, ficar sobrecarregado. Ter que is literally to have that and means must, with a plain infinitive after it.

Measure and frequency. Pelo menos is by the least (pelo is por plus o) and means at least. De vez em quando (of time in when) means once in a while. Por cento is per hundred, percent. Sem falta is without lack, without fail. Deixar tudo pra última hora is to leave everything for the last hour, until the last minute. Vale metade da nota is is worth half of the grade. Isso mesmo is that same, exactly.

Fillers and particles. Né is não é said quickly and tags a sentence like isn't it. Pra is para shortened in speech, and pro is para plus o. These forms are normal in speech and informal writing, and you will not find them in formal notices.

grammar.title: Required, optional or colloquial?
grammar.explanation:
The personal infinitive is partly grammar and partly style. Written Portuguese treats it as the normal way to express a plural or first person doer, especially after prepositions: in laws, contracts, school regulations, notices and news, you will see it on nearly every page. In everyday speech it is often replaced. Register is the level of formality of a way of speaking or writing, and this structure is a clear marker of it.

The most important everyday alternative is a gente. Grammatically a gente is third person singular (a gente precisa), so its personal infinitive is the bare infinitive, and pra gente sair cedo is correct, not a shortcut. The second alternative is to use a conjunction and the subjunctive instead of a preposition and the infinitive: para que eles cheguem, depois que eles chegarem (future subjunctive, for future events), antes que eles saiam. These are complete clauses and are fully standard; they are a little longer, and speakers choose them when they want to keep the verbs more visible.

The third alternative is to drop the ending: Pra eles chegar cedo. You will hear this often in casual speech, and it is normally marked as an error in writing and on exams, so do not use it in anything formal. Some sentences need no alternative at all: É melhor vocês irem is as natural in speech as in writing.

A practical rule: recognize the personal infinitive everywhere, produce it confidently after a preposition when the doer is nós, vocês or eles, and in conversation feel free to switch to a gente with the bare infinitive or to a clause with the subjunctive. If the doer is singular, nothing changes because the form looks the same.

culture.title: Formal writing and school life in Brazil
culture.text:
The personal infinitive is a characteristic feature of Portuguese, and Brazilian formal writing uses it heavily. School regulations, workplace memos, contracts and legal texts are full of phrases such as Os alunos devem apresentar o atestado ao retornarem (students must present the certificate when they return) or Pede-se aos moradores para não deixarem objetos no corredor (residents are asked not to leave objects in the corridor; the literal pede-se is asks-itself, the passive form with se). Reading these texts is the best way to get a feel for the structure, even though in conversation people usually find a lighter way to say the same thing.

School life also explains much of the vocabulary in this unit. Brazilian students must attend at least seventy-five percent of classes to pass the year, which is why the word frequência is so important and why teachers call the roll at the start of class (fazer a chamada, literally to make the call). Enrollment (matrícula) usually takes place in December and January, before the school year starts in February. Universities and companies often ask for group projects (trabalhos em grupo), where dividing tasks fairly is a classic source of complaints.

In the workplace, punctuality is valued but treated with some flexibility, especially outside the big cities where traffic can be unpredictable. Many teams have an informal agreement with the boss (um combinado, literally a combined thing) about flexible arrival times. Still, in formal notices the tone is polite and firm: Solicitamos a todos que cumpram o horário (we ask everyone to keep to the schedule) or Pedimos a gentileza de chegarem no horário (we ask the kindness of you arriving on time, that is, please arrive on time).

paragraphs.en: If there are questions, those concerned only need to contact the personnel department. We thank everyone for their cooperation. Sincerely, the Management.
paragraphs.literal: Case there-be doubts, suffices the interested to-look-for-they the department of personnel. We-thank the collaboration of all. Cordially, the Directorship.

questions.prompt: What is the new arrival time rule?
choices: Arrival is flexible between eight and ten, but eight hours must be worked
Arrival is flexible and no hours are required
questions.explanation: The notice says the entrance time is flexible, but the colleagues must complete the eight daily hours.

questions.prompt: What must employees do before going on vacation?
choices: Ask the interns to replace them
questions.explanation: Antes de saírem de férias, they must comunicar à chefia com trinta dias de antecedência.

questions.prompt: What should interns do when they arrive?
questions.explanation: Ao chegarem à empresa, they sign the lista de presença.

questions.prompt: Where should employees go with questions about the new rules?
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says to procurar o departamento de pessoal.

questions.prompt: In 'Antes de saírem de férias, os funcionários devem comunicar...', who is the subject of saírem?
questions.explanation: The one who leaves on vacation is os funcionários, so saírem takes -em. The main verb devem also has os funcionários as its subject, so the ending is optional here and is used for the formal, explicit style of the notice.

exercises.prompt: In 'É melhor vocês irem', why does irem take the ending -em?
choices: Because irem has its own doer, vocês, and that doer is plural
Because é melhor always needs a plural verb
Because every infinitive after é takes -em
exercises.explanation: The ending records who does the action of the infinitive. Vocês takes third person plural forms, so the infinitive takes -em.
Eles is the subject of both devem and chegar, and dever is a modal verb, so the two verbs work as one unit and the infinitive stays plain.

exercises.prompt: In 'Pedi aos alunos para entregarem o trabalho', who is the subject of entregarem?
exercises.explanation: The subject of an infinitive is whoever does the action, whatever their role in the main clause. The students hand in the work, so the ending is -em.

exercises.prompt: What is the personal infinitive of ser for nós?
exercises.explanation: Add -mos to the whole infinitive: ser plus mos. Formos is the future subjunctive, somos is the present and fôssemos is the imperfect subjunctive.

exercises.prompt: Why does saírem carry an accent, while sairmos does not?
choices: Because eles is plural and nós is not
In saírem the í is alone in its syllable (sa-Í-rem), but in sairmos the r closes it (sa-IR-mos)
Because saírem is stressed on the first syllable
Because the accent marks the nasal sound of em
exercises.explanation: A stressed i directly after another vowel is written í when it stands alone in its syllable, and plain i when r, l, m, n, z or nh closes the syllable. The r moves to the next syllable in saírem, but stays in sairmos.

exercises.prompt: Where does the stress fall in falarem?
exercises.explanation: The stressed vowel is the a that was already stressed in falar. The ending em defaults to the second to last syllable, so no accent is written, unlike também, which is stressed on its last syllable.

exercises.prompt: English says 'for them to leave', with the object form them. How does Portuguese show the doer?
choices: Para os sair, with the object pronoun os
Para deles saírem, with the possessive deles
Para eles saírem, with the subject pronoun eles and the ending -em
Para lhes sair, with the indirect object lhes
exercises.explanation: The doer of an infinitive is its subject, so Portuguese uses the subject form eles, and the ending -em agrees with it like the ending of a finite verb.

exercises.prompt: Which is the natural colloquial alternative to 'Para nós sairmos cedo'?
exercises.explanation: A gente is grammatically third person singular, so its personal infinitive is the bare form sair.

exercises.prompt: Why does horário carry a written accent?
choices: Because the ending io counts as two syllables, so the stress is third to last, which no ending predicts
To tell it apart from horária
exercises.explanation: Ho-RÁ-ri-o is stressed on the third to last syllable. The default rule only predicts last or second to last, so the mark is required.

exercises.prompt: How is the qu in frequência pronounced?
choices: [k], the u is silent as in que
exercises.explanation: Before e, qu is normally [k] with a silent u, but a handful of words keep the sounded u. Until 2009 a trema marked them (freqüência); the reform removed the mark but not the sound.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct in careful formal writing?
choices: Antes de ele chegar, arrumamos a sala.
Antes dele chegar, arrumamos a sala.
Antes de ele chegarem, arrumamos a sala.
exercises.explanation: The subject pronoun ele stays apart from de in careful writing (dele would be the possessive). Ele is singular, so the infinitive stays plain and chegarem is wrong.

exercises.prompt_pt: Antes de nós ___ de casa, conferimos tudo.
exercises.hint_en: Before we left the house, we checked everything.
exercises.explanation: Sair plus mos. The r closes the syllable (sa-IR-mos), so no accent is written.

exercises.prompt_pt: Avisamos a chefia antes de eles ___ do escritório.
exercises.hint_en: We told management before they left the office.
exercises.explanation: Sair plus em. The r moves to the next syllable, leaving the stressed í alone (sa-Í-rem), so the accent is required.

exercises.prompt_pt: Depois de os alunos ___ a prova, o professor saiu.
exercises.hint_en: After the students handed in the exam, the teacher left.
exercises.explanation: The doer os alunos is plural, so the infinitive takes -em. The de stays apart from os because os alunos is the subject.

exercises.prompt_pt: É importante os pais ___ as regras da escola.
exercises.hint_en: It is important for parents to know the school rules.
exercises.explanation: The infinitive has its own plural doer, os pais, so it takes -em.

exercises.prompt_pt: Fizemos uma lista para ninguém ___ nada.
exercises.hint_en: We made a list so that nobody forgets anything.
exercises.explanation: Ninguém is singular, so the personal infinitive looks like the plain infinitive.

exercises.prompt_pt: Eu vi os meninos ___ no prédio.
exercises.hint_en: I saw the boys go into the building.
exercises.explanation: After a perception verb with a noun as the doer, both forms are accepted.

exercises.prompt_pt: Por não ___ avisado o cliente, tivemos problemas.
exercises.hint_en: Because we did not warn the client, we had problems.
exercises.explanation: In the compound infinitive the ending goes on the auxiliary ter, and the participle avisado stays unchanged.

exercises.prompt_pt: Os funcionários devem ___ o contrato hoje.
exercises.hint_en: The employees must sign the contract today.
exercises.explanation: Dever is a modal verb and os funcionários is the subject of both verbs, so the second verb stays plain.

exercises.hint_en: They left without us noticing anything.
exercises.explanation: Nós is the doer of the infinitive, so perceber takes -mos.

exercises.prompt_pt: Para ___ aprovados, os alunos precisam de presença.
exercises.hint_en: To be approved, the students need attendance.
exercises.explanation: The doers are os alunos, plural, so ser takes -em. The participle aprovados agrees with them.

exercises.prompt_en: It is important for us to arrive on time.
answers: É importante chegarmos no horário.
É importante nós chegarmos no horário.
É importante chegarmos na hora.
É importante nós chegarmos na hora.
É importante a gente chegar no horário.
É importante a gente chegar na hora.
exercises.explanation: The doer is us, so the infinitive takes -mos (or the bare form with a gente).

answers: Eu vi as crianças brincarem.
Vi as crianças brincarem.
Eu vi as crianças brincando.
Vi as crianças brincando.
Eu vi as crianças brincar.
Vi as crianças brincar.
exercises.explanation: After a perception verb with a noun as the doer, both infinitive forms occur, and the gerund also works.

exercises.prompt_en: The students must hand in the assignment.
answers: Os alunos devem entregar o trabalho.
Os alunos precisam entregar o trabalho.
Os alunos têm que entregar o trabalho.
Os alunos devem entregar a tarefa.
Os alunos precisam entregar a tarefa.
Os alunos têm que entregar a tarefa.
Os alunos têm de entregar o trabalho.
Os alunos têm de entregar a tarefa.
exercises.explanation: Os alunos is the subject of both verbs, and dever is a modal verb, so the infinitive stays plain.

answers: Antes de sairmos, vamos conversar.
Antes de nós sairmos, vamos conversar.
Antes de a gente sair, vamos conversar.
Antes de sairmos, vamos falar.
Antes de nós sairmos, vamos falar.
exercises.explanation: Antes de plus the personal infinitive. With a gente the bare form is used.

exercises.prompt_en: It is better for you to go now.
exercises.explanation: Vocês is a plural doer, so the infinitive takes -em.

exercises.prompt_en: Upon arriving, the interns sign the list.
exercises.explanation: Ao plus the personal infinitive, with the plural doer os estagiários.

exercises.prompt_en: To finish on time, we need to divide the tasks.
exercises.explanation: The first infinitive has the doer nós and takes -mos; after the modal precisamos the infinitive dividir stays plain.

exercises.prompt_en: The team asked them to send the data.
exercises.explanation: Eles is the doer of enviar, so it takes -em.

exercises.audio_pt: É importante vocês chegarem no horário.
choices: It is important for you to arrive on time.
It is important for you to leave early.
It was important for you to arrive late.
exercises.explanation: Chegarem is arrive, and no horário is on time.

exercises.audio_pt: Depois de terminarmos o trabalho, saímos juntos.
choices: Before we finished the work, we went out together.
After they finished the work, they went out together.
After we finished the work, we went out together.
exercises.explanation: Depois de is after, and terminarmos has the ending -mos, so the doer is we.

exercises.audio_pt: Os estagiários devem assinar a lista ao chegarem.
choices: The managers must sign the list when they arrive.
The interns must sign the list when they arrive.
The interns must sign the list before leaving.
exercises.explanation: Ao chegarem is upon arriving, and os estagiários are the interns.

exercises.audio_pt: Pedi para eles enviarem os documentos.
choices: They asked me to send the documents.
I asked you to send the documents.
I asked them to sign the documents.
I asked them to send the documents.
exercises.explanation: Pedi is I asked, eles enviarem is for them to send.

exercises.hint_en: It is better for them to leave now.
exercises.explanation: Saírem keeps the accent on the í.

exercises.audio_pt: Para fazermos a matrícula, precisamos dos documentos.
exercises.hint_en: To do the enrollment, we need the documents.
exercises.explanation: Fazermos is fazer plus mos.

exercises.audio_pt: Sem vocês ajudarem, não vamos terminar.
exercises.hint_en: Without you helping, we won't finish.
exercises.explanation: Ajudarem is ajudar plus em, with the doer vocês.

exercises.prompt: Match the verbs with their meanings
exercises.explanation: Recall of this unit's verbs.

exercises.prompt: Match each form with the doer it shows

pairs.en: before you arrive, speaking to one person as tu

exercises.explanation: -mos is nós, -em is eles, -es is tu, and the bare form is a singular doer.
